items.title: Michael Nielsen took down his book on neural nets
items.content:
I wrote this book between 2011 and 2015. At the time, I expected AGI systems based on neural networks to be many decades away, but to bring remarkable benefits for humanity. I also expected significant challenges, but believed it likely that, as with other technologies, those challenges would be addressed as the capabilities were developed.

My views have changed. With the extraordinarily reckless behaviour of the frontier labs, the systems have raced ahead much faster than I expected 1 , giving humanity far too little time to meet the challenges. Although the systems genuinely will bring — indeed, already are bringing — many wonders, they also pose a significant risk of catastrophe. The frontier labs are knowingly endangering all of humanity. I've written about why I believe this at length , most recently in “Which Future?” . Two brief thoughts are below.

I don't wish to help (even in a very small way) train people to contribute to this work, and so I've taken the book down.

What follows are two brief remarks: one on the nature of the threat posed by ASI, and another on the ethical justification for working on frontier AI.

The most common argument for AI existential risk, developed by Nick Bostrom and Eliezer Yudkowsky, is loss of control of the future to advanced AI systems 2 . I believe this concern should be understood as one instance of a more fundamental issue. That issue is whether we will discover technologies latent in nature which are easy and inexpensive to develop, catastrophic in outcome, and beyond our capacity to defend against. If such “progress” in technology were happening slowly, our social institutions might successfully develop defences. But it seems likely that ASI will cause a sudden explosion of such destructive technologies, with insufficient time to adapt.

A historical example to help prime intuition is fire. It is easy to make and extremely difficult to defend against. We have a one-cent technology, the matchstick, which requires hundreds of billions of dollars each year to defend against, as well as a whole apparatus of social institutions, technology, infrastructure and law 3 . AI systems will enable technologies which are far more destructive than matches. Understandably, people skeptical of catastrophic risks want these supposed threats spelled out in detail. This is intrinsically difficult, because we can't reliably anticipate future science and technology. While it is common to speculate about biothreats, I expect the worst threats will be technologies we haven't yet imagined. Nature is, after all, more imaginative than we.

Now suppose that ASI enables a 100-times speed-up in technological progress, without a matching change in the rate of social progress or social defenses. To get a sense of what the impact of such a speed-up would be, imagine that all the technological problems that occurred in the 20th century had occurred in the year 1901: the atomic bomb, the hydrogen bomb, the ICBM, chemical weapons, biological weapons, the CFC-caused ozone hole, sulfuric acid rain, climate change, and many more. While we've dealt well with some of these problems, it required decades of concerted work to develop the social institutions and agreements needed for an effective response. Again, defence is often much harder than offence, and relies on different systems. Of course, such a speed-up would also have brought the century's wonders all at once. But imagine another such set of equally difficult problems arising in 1902, and then 1903, and then 1904, and so on. I believe it would have made the world extraordinarily unstable and eventually liable to collapse.

The issue with ASI, then, is the destructive power latent in nature. It doesn't matter whether that power is wielded by humans or by out-of-control machines 4 . I make this point because many people mistakenly believe that loss of control to such rogue machines is the fundamental issue. This leads them to treat AI safety as principally a…

items.title: Hard Drive pricing has gotten bad
items.summary: hardware
items.content:
For years now, I’ve made it an annual tradition to replace one or two hard drives on Black Friday. I typically run around ten physical disks, and swapping a couple out each year means I almost never have a drive older than five years in my systems. I’ve even previously made videos about shucking disks around this time of year .

But current hardware pricing is totally screwed. So what is a lifelong self-hoster to do in times like these? With disk capacities increasing massively over the last 10 years I can now fit 20TB per slot. This means I could realistically go from ten spinners to five, and not really feel it too acutely. This will mean redoing my zpool layouts, which in turn means shuffling some data around as ZFS doesn’t like changes to the layout of existing pools. But, at these prices, I’m starting to think the hassle might be worth it.

Let’s take a look at disk prices over the past 8 years in today’s post.

The 20TB WD EasyStore I bought for $249.99 in November 2024 is, today, on sale, $549.99 this Black Friday. $300 more than 2 years ago for the same product, from the same store. It shows just how bad hard drive pricing has gotten ( BestBuy 20TB listing ).

Shucking is homelab speak for taking a perfectly good external drive out of its USB enclosure and sticking the SATA drive in your server. At $12.50/TB it was a fantastically affordable way to get massive amounts of storage. At $27.50/TB, absolutely not.

In November 2018 I bought five 10TB EasyStores for $179.99 each. At the time I wrote about doing the rounds of my local Best Buys to pickup more drives on Black Friday as quantities were limited at each location ( My 2018 server build log ).

October 2023 was my best haul on a per-TB basis. Three 18TB drives put 54TB in my hands for $599.97. This year’s “deal” is fifty bucks shy of that entire order . Best Buy was still advertising those 18TB drives for $199.99 in November 2023. November 2023 deal archive

WD EasyStore 20TB, SKU 6500985. Prices are before tax.

Buying refurbished or recertified enterprise drives used to be an easy way to bring the cost down. In August 2024 I bought four recertified 14TB Ultrastars from ServerPartDeals for $529.96 before tax . That was 56TB at $9.46/TB , even cheaper than the EasyStores and no shucking to do.

US dollars per TB. Hatched bars mark equivalent sold-out listings as of Nov 2026.

Drive 2024 price per drive Nov 26, 2026 listing Change per TB

WD Ultrastar HC530 14TB 4Kn, recertified ( WUH721414ALN604 ) $129.99 · $9.29/TB $204.99 · $14.64/TB · Sold out +58%

WD Ultrastar HC530 14TB 512e, recertified ( WUH721414ALE6L4 ) $134.99 · $9.64/TB $429.00 · $30.64/TB · Sold out +218%

Seagate Exos X20 20TB, refurbished ( ST20000NM007D ) $235.94 · $11.80/TB $589.00 · $29.45/TB · In stock +150%

Seagate Exos X22 20TB, recertified ( ST20000NM004E ) $224.99 · $11.25/TB · later refunded $649.00 · $32.45/TB · Sold out +188%

The sad truth is that across the board prices are up a minimum of 58%, and sometimes as much as 218% in just a year or two.

When the EasyStore is that bad, my first instinct is to shop around. Maybe I should try another retailer (to be clear I’m not blaming BestBuy for any of this), buy an enterprise drive, see what’s available recertified. But follow those listings back to the companies that actually make the drives and the choices narrow pretty quickly. There are three big HDD makers left. How did we end up with so few?

Maxtor bought Quantum’s hard drive business in 2001, then Seagate bought Maxtor in 2006. Hitachi combined IBM’s disk business with its own to form HGST in 2003, and Toshiba bought Fujitsu’s HDD business in 2009. Seagate bought Samsung’s HDD business in December 2011, and Western Digital bought HGST in March 2012. The FTC required WD to sell desktop-drive manufacturing assets to Toshiba to keep a third supplier in that market. That left Seagate, Western Digital and Toshiba.

items.title: Google told to halt Belgium datacentre construction over lack of planning permit
items.content:
‘Inspectors visited the site and observed that the building was almost finished … even though the permit had been refused,’ a regional official said. Photograph: Nicolas Tucat/AFP/Getty

‘Inspectors visited the site and observed that the building was almost finished … even though the permit had been refused,’ a regional official said. Photograph: Nicolas Tucat/AFP/Getty

Google told to halt Belgium datacentre construction over lack of planning permit

Greenpeace publishes report showing tech firm is continuing to build despite planning appeal still unresolved

Belgian authorities have ordered Google to halt construction work on a large datacentre in the south of the country because the US tech firm’s requests to modify the original terms of the planning permission did not have approval.

“Inspectors visited the site and observed that the building was almost finished, with the structural work completed, even though the permit had been refused,” Raphaël Stokis, a Wallonia regional official, told the public broadcaster RTBF .

Stokis said the 300 workers had been given a verbal order to stop work that had been confirmed in writing to Google. The company said in a statement it was “committed to maintaining an open and collaborative dialogue” with the regional authorities.

Google’s 2025 application to change its plans, notably including a switch from air to water cooling, was initially approved by local authorities but later revoked after protests. The company has appealed and a ruling is due early next year.

The vast building, which occupies about 3 hectares (7.4 acres) of a 50-hectare business park on the site of a former coalmine at Aiseau-Presles, about 15km (9 miles) west of Charleroi, is one of three originally planned by Google on the site.

The Google construction site. Photograph: Belga News Agency/Alamy Nicolas Yernaux, a regional government spokesperson, told Agence France-Presse on Friday that a report was being submitted to public prosecutors alleging “a major offence: the illegal construction of a building covering 3 hectares”.

The environmental group Greenpeace earlier this week published a report including drone footage that showed Google was carrying on construction work at the site despite lacking the correct permits.

“The tech giant is continuing work, even though in August the latest version of its planning permission to build this datacentre was revoked,” Greenpeace said, adding that it had filed an emergency appeal with local planning authorities.

“The climate crisis will only intensify in our region,” the environmental group said. “Against this backdrop, the construction of energy-guzzling behemoths cannot be allowed to go unnoticed.”

How datacentres are driving an illegal mining rush in the Amazon ‘more devastating than gold’

Google’s 2024 permit was to construct three smaller air-cooled datacentres, but in 2025 it applied instead to merge two of them into one much larger facility and switch to liquid cooling by drawing 600m3 of water an hour from the nearby Sambre River.

The regional administration initially approved the amendments in April, but residents and protest groups appealed and in August the Wallonia infrastructure minister, François Desquesnes, revoked the modified permit over drought concerns.

Google appealed against that decision to Belgium’s council of state and a ruling in the case is expected on 7 January. A company spokesperson said on Friday: “We have halted works consistent with the direction from local authorities and pending additional guidance.

“We have operated in Belgium for over 15 years and remain committed to complying with local laws and an open, collaborative dialogue with government officials and all relevant authorities about our work in Wallonia.”

The legal row is the latest confronting the company in Europe as large tech companies push to build datacentres to support the AI boom.

items.content:
All the sites we contacted took action; but the larger consumer web ecosystem should be prepared to mitigate these attack vectors

A card-skimming script was planted on the online stores of Lascana, Samsonite, American Tourister, Revolve and FWRD in the week before Black Friday. After our reports to affected companies, all have had the script removed (on November 24th or 25th) ahead of Black Friday. We observed it in action on one of the five websites: Lascana, where it sent our test card's details to a 3rd party. We believe the script was built to take a card number, expiry and security code, along with a user's name, address, phone and email, and send them to malefactors as a user entered their payment credentials. It did this before the store checked the payment, so a card could be taken even if the order was declined or cancelled, and nothing would look wrong to the shopper. Across all of these sites, we do not know how many, if any, shopper details or payment credentials may have been captured.

items.title: Objections to .php application being published on ICANN site
items.summary: web
items.content:
.php written in Handel Gothic italic, dark brown text on yellow background.

After Automattic's confirmation that they would switch their .vibe application to the replacement string of .php 1 , ICANN has started to publish various objections on the Application Comment Forum (ACF) section of their new gTLD program site 2 . They mostly relate to the confusion and security risk posed by a common filetype (especially in web development) becoming a TLD, similar to the outcry over Google's application for .zip (which was eventually successfully delegated). The other common theme is the objection to a private company effectively trying to claim what is an open-source project.

The first is by PHP developer Larry Garfield who accused the WordPress parent of "Inappropriate Squatting": 3

PHP is a widely used programming language. It is managed by the PHP project, an informal project at www.php.net . It is also supported by The PHP Foundation, a non-profit organization managed through OpenCollective.

No one organization, company, or person owns or controls PHP. Authority within the PHP language and ecosystem is deliberately diffuse.

Automattic, the company that has attempted to register .php as a TLD, is the owner/author of the WordPress blogging software. WordPress is itself written in PHP and Javascript. However, Automattic has no ownership or control over the PHP language itself. In fact, Automattic and its employees are conspicuously absent from contribution to the PHP project itself, aside from in recent years becoming a large passive donor to The PHP Foundation.

For Automattic, or any other company that operates in the PHP space, to try and lay claim to .php as a TLD is grossly inappropriate. There are dozens of other companies, projects, and interested parties that have just as much if not more claim to the name. PHP is a far larger ecosystem than just Automattic.

It would be equivalent to Microsoft registering .rust (they use a lot of Rust now, but did not originate the language), or Hashicorp registering .golang, or IBM registering .java. None of those would be reasonable or appropriate, and neither is any one organization owning .php.

One company owning .php would be significantly harmful to the PHP ecosystem, as it would give control over a significant branding and marketing channel to one company that is not engaged in the ecosystem, leading to market confusion and an easily exploitable way for that company to claim more authority and ownership than it actually has.

The only organization that has any legitimate claim to register .php would be The PHP Foundation, but they have made no such attempt.

The application for .php should be rejected outright as inappropriate "domain squatting." Its approval would be detrimental to a major software ecosystem, and establish a dangerous precedent for one company claiming an entire ecosystem's name without cause.

WordPress contributor Jamie VanRaalte objected on the grounds of "Part of a pattern - .php should not go to one company" and also said the .wordpress application was a similarly inappropriate power grab of another open-source project: 4

I agree with the comments already made here about .php. [I've been building commercial software in PHP for X years.] PHP is run by the PHP project and supported by The PHP Foundation, and no company owns it.

I want to add one thing that's easy to miss when this application is looked at on its own. Knock Knock WHOIS There, LLC is a subsidiary of Automattic, and it has also applied for .wordpress. WordPress is an open source project too, and its trademark is held by the WordPress Foundation, not Automattic. So this is one company applying for the names of two open source ecosystems that it takes part in but does not govern.

Automattic does use PHP heavily, but so do millions of other developers and companies. Using a language doesn't give a company any claim to its name. If .php goes to Automattic, it would decide who can register under…

items.title: Incident Report: unsanctioned agent behaviour during cyber testing | AISI Work
items.content:
You can access the full technical report here.

AISI’s role is to evaluate and understand the capabilities of frontier AI models, surfacing potential risks before they reach the public. To assess what these models can do, including whether they could be misused for cyberattacks, we test them under deliberately permissive conditions: with access to the open internet, and with some safety filters disabled.

On 28 th July 2026, AISI's Security Team detected unusual data transfers leaving our research systems during a routine cyber evaluation. On investigation, we found that some of the agents being tested had engaged in sustained, potentially harmful activity directed at real people and organisations. We declared a security incident and, within roughly one hour of discovery, had contained it and begun a full investigation.

The incident stemmed from a single evaluation where agents were given a task of solving a cyber security challenge. We ran this challenge 122 times across several models. Our investigation found that in 10 of those runs, an AI agent took autonomous, unsanctioned action on the live internet, targeting real people and organisations. In total, we catalogued 19 such actions. Almost all of this behaviour (17 actions) came from a single model, Anthropic's Mythos 5, with 2 actions involving OpenAI's GPT-5.6-Sol with cyber classifiers (mechanisms to prevent misuse) disabled. In the most serious case, an agent tried to insert malicious code into an open-source project. In an attempt to get the code approved, the agent engaged in social engineering  — creating fake online identities and using them to pressure the project's maintainer to approve the code. A human maintainer caught and refused to approve the malicious code.

These attempts were unsuccessful, and our investigations have not evidenced any resulting real-world harm. But this is the first time we have seen risks around autonomy and deception manifest this clearly, without specific prompting, in the real-world.

Importantly, this was not a case of a model escaping its secure test environment, or ‘sandbox’. As was standard in our cyber testing, we had intentionally permitted internet access, and model-provider cyber classifiers were deliberately disabled - conditions that do not reflect how frontier models are made available to the public. We do this to best assess the maximum capability of models. These configuration choices have been common practice in frontier AI evaluations. The specific models in question, in the configurations in which we tested them are not commercially available and there is no clear indication of similar activity outside of testing scenarios.

Ahead of publishing this blog, we notified GitHub (the developer platform accessed during the evaluation) of the agents' malicious activity, which included actions that GitHub has confirmed violated their terms of service. We worked together with GitHub to remove artefacts left behind by the agent, and to notify the GitHub users the model interacted with. We have also contacted other affected parties. We also intend to work with METR (Model Evaluation and Threat Research) to conduct an independent third-party review – we are still working through the scope of this review with them.

This incident should be interpreted with caution and nuance. To some degree, our evaluation design choices and specific configurations enabled the behaviour. Nonetheless, the activity undertaken by the agent show signs of novel, potentially deceptive behaviours, and were to an extent and severity we did not anticipate.

There are important caveats to bear in mind: we observed a small number of events under very specific conditions, and cannot yet say how likely such behaviour is in different contexts or outside of testing environments. items.title: Tidal Bans AI Music, Moves to Delete 29 Million Slop Songs: Human-created music to our ears.
items.content:
The slop janitors are out in full force at Tidal.

The music streaming platform announced that it’s officially banning AI-generated songs starting on December 9. Based on its own estimates, the purge will wipe out an astonishing 29 million AI-generated tracks — and stop a flood of up to 85,000 machine-fabricated songs per day, according to Robert Andersen, Tidal’s head at its parent company Block.

“We believe this will resonate with both artists and listeners alike, as 96 percent of all AI-generated songs receive zero plays at all,” Andersen wrote in a statement on X.

The move makes Tidal the only major music streaming platform to enact a wholesale ban on fully AI-generated songs, escalating its already aggressive stance towards the tech. This summer, it started scanning and labelling tracks that its systems identified as 100 percent AI-generated and demonetized them.

Other platforms have cracked down on AI slop tracks, including Spotify and YouTube, but more in a manner that’s similar to how it would deal with any other form of spam, rather than as a principled stand against the technology. None of them have declared a full stop ban like Tidal has — Bandcamp is an exception, but it’s a distribution platform rather than a proper streamer — and some weave in their own AI features.

Spotify, for example, said it removed more than 50 million songs it deemed AI-generated spam from its recommendation algorithms last month, rather than deleting them entirely. (Slop invading its discovery pages and listener algorithms has been a persistent problem .) It has also balked at slapping tracks with AI labels, as platforms like YouTube Music have done, and is reportedly readying the launch of an AI remixing feature.

Part of Tidal’s rationale was that the deluge of AI tracks was drowning out human artists ; over the past 90 days, over 43 percent of all tracks submitted to the platform were fully AI-generated, which had not Tidal not removed them, would’ve eaten into the revenue pool of real musicians.

“Wholly AI-generated music intended to mislead listeners and impersonate artists is another serious problem that has only increased in scale: It diverts streams and royalties away from the artists, and confuses fans,” it said in a statement .

“It’s true that not all songs catch on immediately, and artists should have time to build their fanbases,” it added. “But this situation is different — at this scale, the authentic music and artists that Tidal subscribers are looking to listen to and discover get buried.”

items.title: GPT 6.2 Astra Solves a Historical Mystery
items.content:
GPT 6.2 Astra Solves a Historical Mystery

OpenAI’s newest model can autonomously research open historical problems from end to end, forming hypotheses to make new discoveries.

There’s a growing sense in the AI community that we’re approaching an intelligence explosion far faster than even the most optimistic accelerationists predicted. One of the most publicly visible signals pointing at that acceleration is the rapid progress made in mathematics in recent months.

In four years, LLMs have gone from scoring a D+ on elementary school math tests to literally solving hundreds of the most difficult problems in the field in the space of only a few weeks—decades of progress compressed into two months. Navier-Stokes, one of the central Millennium Prize Problems posed by the Clay Mathematics Institute more than a quarter century ago, fell in September . Last Friday, Anthropic researcher and mathematician Levent Alpöge announced a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, which paradoxically can be verified using a mathematics program called Lean , but has yet to be understood by human experts. Just last night, Anthropic casually posted a solution to the VP vs VNP problem without any fanfare. Such things are becoming the norm.

Because mathematics is deterministic, though, observers have wondered whether this same process of research and discovery will generalize to non-deterministic domains like history. In this blog post, I will present evidence that this is indeed starting to happen.

I recently had the opportunity to test OpenAI’s new model, GPT-6.2 Astra , before it was released and it made a significant historical discovery. This required it to read through sources, develop a hypothesis with limited evidence, and make an argument. Moreover, it would be unlikely that a human could replicate what it did.

With only minimal prompting, GPT-6.2 Astra was able to autonomously identify the creator of an anonymous 1808 sketchbook held at Yale’s Beinecke Library . It did so extremely quickly (in just 22 minutes), using publicly available primary and secondary sources. To do so, it discovered a little known source in a paper archive, predicted that it would prove its hypothesis if examined and, in the end, it did. Not only that, but this new source turns out to be a major find on its own that will be of significant interest to both Canadian and fur trade historians. While it’s a narrow example, it’s representative of the historical research process as a whole and a sign of things to come.

I started testing GPT-6.2 Astra in late October in the ChatGPT Windows Desktop app. It is a quirky but highly capable model, especially well suited to long-running, open-ended tasks that might take hours or days to complete. I’ve found that its results were remarkably reliable and consistent, allowing me to contemplate tasks that were too difficult or long-running for previous models. For example, I had it examine and correct an 8,002-row CSV transcription of the Shipboy & Henry daybook. Last fall, I was amazed that Gemini 3 Pro could work in pounds, shillings, and pence . GPT-6.2 used the internal math of the ledger to verify and fix transcriptions against 353 images. In essence, it tested the handwritten math across thousands of quantities, item prices, sub-totals and account totals over the course of only a few hours and made edits accordingly. I had previously tried this with both GPT-6 Astra and Fable 5 and neither one completed the task as thoroughly or competently.

Even so, GPT-6.2 Astra sometimes communicates in a weird way, writing backwards-speak, riddle-like answers that seem wrong at first glance but turn out to be technically correct. It often feels like I’m reading a formal legal disclaimer, but one written in a friendly, colloquial way. The strangest thing, though, is that the underlying work product is always sound.

items.title: Google's DeepCrossAttention achieves comparable model quality up to 3x faster
items.content:
Kyriakos Axiotis, Staff Research Scientist, and Thomas Fu, Principal Engineer, Google Research

We present DeepCrossAttention (DCA), an architecture that enhances transformer networks by using learnable weights and depth-wise cross-attention to dynamically combine outputs from previous layers, preventing the information dilution seen in traditional residual connections. Presented in our ICML 2025 paper, this architectural improvement allows models to achieve the same quality up to three times faster with a negligible increase in parameters.

Think of a traditional deep learning model like a giant game of "Telephone": data passes through layer after layer, with each layer changing the information slightly. If a network has dozens or hundreds of layers, the original learning signal can become severely degraded or lost by the time it reaches all layers, which is known as the vanishing gradient problem in AI.

To overcome this challenge and enable the training of networks with dozens or hundreds of layers, transformers rely heavily on residual connections , also known as “skip” connections, which act like an information highway or a shortcut. Instead of forcing the data to pass exclusively through the complicated layer, a duplicate copy of the original input skips right past this layer and is added directly to its output. This ensures that the model always has the original raw data to refer back to.

The standard residual connection implements a simple operation: point-wise summation of a layer's output with its input. While computationally efficient, this simple process has a key limitation: it treats all prior representations with equal weight, leading to information dilution in deep networks. As features propagate through many layers, specific, high-resolution details from earlier layers can be averaged out or distorted, making it difficult for the network to selectively retrieve them. This forces the network to recompute them, reducing learning efficiency.

In our ICML 2025 paper, "DeepCrossAttention: Supercharging Transformer Residual Connections ," we studied the shortcomings of the traditional residual architecture and introduced DeepCrossAttention (DCA), which generalizes residual connections by allowing each layer to dynamically select and route features from the history of preceding layers. By allowing the model to dynamically choose which previous layers are most important at any given moment, DCA achieves comparable or improved learning, while reducing the number of parameters needed by up to 30-40%.

Instead of treating skip connections as a rigid, additive pipeline, DCA reframes residual learning as a dynamic routing problem. Rather than passing all prior layers forward with equal weight, DCA introduces a lightweight, layer-wise module that decides how to best combine previous embeddings on a per-token basis.

While a standard residual network uses rigid, additive point-wise connections with equal weighting, DCA introduces dynamic, learned routing weights (W) that allow each layer to selectively route and combine features from across the history of preceding layers.

By allowing the network to dynamically select and retrieve high-resolution features from earlier layers, DCA eliminates the information dilution inherent to classic residual connections.

To test whether DCA can overcome information dilution in practice, we evaluated our approach across controlled synthetic setups, large-scale language modeling benchmarks, and image classification tasks.

DCA demonstrated significant improvements in convergence speed, training stability, and final model quality across these experiments.

items.title: Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs
items.content:
Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs

Carmaker points finger at an 'unknown' flaw as customer fallout continues

Nissan has joined the growing list of Oracle customers cleaning up after a cyberattack, warning employees that payroll records, bank details, Social Security numbers, and other personal data may have been stolen.

In a filing submitted to the California Attorney General on Friday, Nissan Americas said Oracle had informed it of "a cyber event" involving the personnel records of "hundreds of companies." The automaker said it later learned Nissan had been "specifically targeted" in the attack.

A notification sent to current and former employees, seen by The Register , says the company believes attackers accessed a haul of sensitive info, including contact and banking information; Social Security, Social Insurance, or other national identification numbers; financial and tax records; and dependent and beneficiary details.

Current and former employees in the US, Canada, Mexico, and Brazil may have been affected, although Nissan said it is still working to determine exactly whose information was exposed.

Nissan said it kicked off its incident response plan after learning of the intrusion, brought in outside security specialists, and has been working with Oracle while keeping law enforcement informed. It plans to offer affected individuals credit or dark web monitoring where available.

The company has also put a few extra locks on the payroll office. Employees can now access pay slips or update direct deposit details only from a corporate network or through a secure VPN, while Nissan adds extra identity checks before processing payroll requests.

The accompanying employee FAQ pins the incident on "an unknown vulnerability in Oracle's PeopleSoft software" and says the campaign is affecting "hundreds of companies and institutions." The document offers no clue as to what the vulnerability is, whether Oracle has patched it, or whether the compromised PeopleSoft environment was hosted by Oracle or by Nissan itself.

The disclosure lands just weeks after researchers linked the ShinyHunters extortion crew to a wave of attacks exploiting a PeopleSoft zero-day . More than 100 organizations and roughly 300 PeopleSoft instances were reportedly compromised before Oracle issued mitigation measures, with the gang claiming to have made off with HR, payroll, and other enterprise data.

Weak security means attackers could disable all of a city's public EV chargers

US regulator tells GM to hit the brakes on customer tracking

Oracle has said little publicly about the reported attacks and didn't respond to The Register's questions, even as organizations have continued to disclose being caught in the fallout.

Nissan has not confirmed that the incidents are connected, though its California filing lists the breach period as May 27 through June 9, broadly aligning with the previously reported timeline.

The carmaker didn't respond to questions about how many current and former employees are affected, when Oracle first notified it of the breach, and whether the compromise was limited to Oracle-managed systems. ®

Attorneys General Jones and Rayfield File Suit Against SpaceX, Parent Company of X, xAI, and Grok, Over Creation and Promotion of Child Exploitation and Non-Consensual Images on Platform

Virginia and Oregon Attorneys General seek accountability for harms and significant new protections for consumers

RICHMOND, Va . – Today, Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones took a significant step in holding operators of X and its AI tool, Grok, accountable for knowingly failing to protect Virginians, while falsely promoting the safety of its platform and AI tool.

In the lawsuit , the Commonwealth of Virginia alleges that SpaceX, the telecommunications and space transportation conglomerate that operates the social network X and its artificial intelligence company, xAI (now called “SpaceX Super Intelligence”), and developed the Grok family of large language models, failed to prevent Grok from generating sexualized images of people, including children, without their knowledge or consent—while simultaneously promoting the safety of the social media platform and AI tool. The Grok-generated content includes non-consensual intimate imagery (NCII), other non-consensual sexualized images, and Child Sexual Abuse Material (CSAM). Today’s suit was filed in collaboration with Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield, who filed a separate but similar action.

“This lawsuit is about seeking justice for the millions of Virginians who maintain accounts on X and were misled by the company’s false reassurances that their data and images would be safe on the platform,” said Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones. “When xAI allowed Grok’s creators to sideline consent to turn a profit, they prioritized growth and engagement over safety, and they deceived the public about it. Today’s filings are the first step towards holding this company accountable.”

With a single existing photograph, Grok could, and did, fabricate a realistic image or video of a person nude, or partially nude, or engaged in sexual activity, all without the individual’s knowledge or consent.  This violation is not acceptable.

The company ignored industry-standard safeguards so xAI could distinguish itself in the AI arms race. Grok’s ability to generate sexualized content was leveraged as a promotional opportunity. These exploitations of Virginian’s safety enabled the widespread creation and distribution of sexualized images through Grok’s integration with X.

“SpaceX allowed Grok and the X platform to create, host, and share unacceptable and dangerous content—and in fact knowingly designed a product without the obviously necessary safeguards in place,” said Attorney General Rayfield. “It’s no surprise that Grok and X became a haven for perpetrators using AI to create and share child sexual abuse material. The lack of needed safety measures was considered a feature, not a bug, which they promoted as ‘spicy mode.’”

In his filing, Attorney General Jones shows that SpaceX and its subsidiaries marketed Grok as an AI companion with a “rebellious streak,” knowing that its video and image generation technology would be used to produce CSAM, non-consensual intimate images of adults and children (NCII), and other sexualized imagery. In fact, X and its subsidiaries created and promoted a “spicy mode” that specifically allowed for the creation of nude and otherwise sexualized images.

A study by the Center for Countering Digital Harm (“CCDH”) estimated that, between December 29, 2025, and January 8, 2026, Grok created and posted on X approximately three million sexualized images, including approximately 23,000 images that appeared to depict children. That’s an average pace of roughly 190 sexualized images per minute, and one sexualized image of a child approximately every 41 seconds. items.title: Chinese Hackers Abused Google Workspace Rules to Steal Research and Defense Emails
items.content:
A China-linked espionage group hid inside North American medical, academic, and military research networks for more than a year, quietly stealing sensitive research and defense email.

The way in was a backdoor on their REDCap research servers that stole login credentials. The exfiltration was the unusual part: the attackers rewired the victims' own Google Workspace rules to copy any message matching their keywords to an inbox they controlled.

Google's Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) laid out the campaign in a report published this week and attributes it with high confidence to a cluster it tracks as UNC6508.

The actor and its REDCap backdoor are not new names; Google first surfaced both in February , in a wider report on state-backed attacks against the defense sector. It did not name the victims, describing them only as multiple organizations across the US and Canada: clinical providers, academic centers, military health institutions, advocacy groups, and health regulators.

Google says it notified them and disrupted the group's infrastructure.

The entry point was REDCap (Research Electronic Data Capture), a web platform that hospitals and universities use to build and manage study databases. UNC6508 compromised externally facing REDCap servers.

Google has not pinned down the initial access vector, named a specific CVE, or listed the affected versions, though it saw the group probing older, vulnerable ones.

Around three months after getting in, the group deployed custom malware GTIG calls INFINITERED , which trojanizes REDCap's own system files and does three things.

The earliest known compromise dates to September 2023, with activity continuing through November 2025. Once on the server, UNC6508 ran internal reconnaissance and credential discovery, pulling database and service account credentials, then used those logins to move into the internal network and on to a domain administrator account.

Google does not spell out the exact path to that admin account. With admin rights, the group set up the exfiltration.

The exfiltration rode a feature that was already there. UNC6508 abused content compliance rules, a legitimate Google Workspace admin feature that scans mail for keywords and can copy or forward matching messages.

Similar features exist in other cloud mail suites. The group created a rule, misspelled "Patroit," that watched for nearly 150 keywords, search terms, and email addresses. When a message matched, Workspace silently BCC'd it to an attacker-controlled Gmail address, which Google has since disabled. No malware on the mail server, no separate exfiltration tool, no unusual network traffic. Just a built-in mail feature, turned to copy the organization's secrets to an inbox the attackers owned.

MITRE already catalogs email-forwarding-rule abuse as a known technique. What GTIG flags as new here is the use of domain content compliance rules to do it, a method it says it had not seen from a China-linked actor before.

The rule's keywords mapped to UNC6508's collection priorities: geo-strategic policy, military strategy and equipment, advanced technology including AI and uncrewed vehicles, offensive cyber programs, and medical research. One term stood out for its specificity, chikungunya , the mosquito-borne virus behind a 2025 outbreak in China's Guangdong province.

Start with REDCap. Patch externally facing servers and remove old versions outright, not just alongside the current build. REDCap lets legacy versions run side-by-side, and that is what enables downgrade attacks, where an attacker forces software back to a known-vulnerable release.

Then check the mail side. Review Workspace, or equivalent, content compliance and mail-forwarding rules for anything that BCCs or reroutes mail to outside addresses. items.title: The Balatro Timeline
items.content:
It’s been approximately 3 years since I began work on Balatro - and in that time I have personally documented almost nothing about the journey. This is something that has bothered me since the game launched. I am constantly forgetting major moments in development or milestones. It’s about time I start writing down what happened, I say better late than never!

This is an account of everything related to Balatro development in chronological order, up to and including the launch day. This should tell the story but more importantly it will serve as a source of truth for me when I look back on this time in a few years to recall the details correctly. I already notice talking to friends, players, and media that I contradict myself on some of the details from time to time. I’ll try and keep this up to date as I remember more about what happened.

This is the creation date for template , a folder in my Learning/Lua/ directory. This is the creation of the project that would eventually become Balatro.

I had saved up about 3 weeks of vacation time from my IT job, and since they didn’t allow people to accrue vacation year over year I just took off a bunch of time in December to work on some kind of project. At the very beginning of this time off I was working on a game called Autohike . I had been working on this game for a few months at this point but I wasn’t really feeling it anymore, so very early into my vacation I pivoted to cleaning up the code I had created and making a template for a new game.

The initial idea on Dec 13th was to create an online multiplayer version of Big Cheat , a game that a few friends and I had invented many years prior and played a ton based on the card games Big 2 and Cheat .

This whole first week was mostly me trying to upgrade the engine I built with Autohike to better fit a card game.

This is the creation date for CardGame , my current production working folder for all Balatro source code. I never bothered changing the name.

I remember spending a long time making custom pixel art for the red deck back and all the playing cards. It was the first time I had tried making proper pixel art.

I had a very weird prototype. There were no Jokers, there were no blinds to select, the upgrade system consisted of randomly choosing a card from the deck and slapping a weird ‘enhancement’ on it. But it definitely had the bones of Balatro at this point, so it was pretty clear that I abandoned the online Big Cheat idea immediately.

The game had the CHIP X MULT mechanic already. I really don’t know where this idea came from but it seemed very natural for a scoring system. Earlier in December I was watching videos of Luck Be a Landlord from Northernlion and that whole score attack concept really fuelled the direction I wanted to go with this game from this point onward.

I also made a very conscious effort not to play any more roguelike games starting now. I want to be crystal clear here and say that this was not because I thought it would result in a better game , this was because making games is my hobby, releasing them and making money from them is not, so naively exploring roguelike design (and especially deckbuilder design, since I had never played one before) was part of the fun for me. I wanted to make mistakes, I wanted to reinvent the wheel, I didn’t want to borrow tried-and-true designs from existing games. That likely would have resulted in a more tight game but it would have defeated the purpose of what I love about making games.

I started sharing progress with a few of my friends, but no builds were shared yet.

My vacation is over, but I am now fully immersed and obsessed . This is my favourite feeling in the world. When I was back in University I would routinely stay up until the wee hours of the morning working on my weird game projects and greet my parents while they made their morning coffee. I got back into this groove and starting in January I was hooked.

Evenings and weekends were Joker Poker…

items.title: HP Poly VoIP vulnerability sets the stage for executive voice deepfakes
items.content:
HP has released patches for a critical buffer overflow vulnerability in multiple IP-enabled conference phones from its Poly Voice line. The flaw allows unauthenticated attackers to obtain root privileges on the underlying operating system, potentially enabling them to execute other attacks such as eavesdropping on conversations and recording voice data for AI-enabled impersonation attacks.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-0826 , was discovered by researchers from security firm Rapid7 and resides in the code that parses Session Description Protocol (SDP) attributes when the Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) feature is enabled.

ICE enables VoIP devices to establish peer-to-peer connections using the shortest available network path. The feature is not enabled by default on HP Poly devices, and the company advises administrators to disable it if it’s not needed.

The flaw, rated 9.2 on the CVSS severity scale, affects all phones from the HP Poly VVX series, as well as the Trio 8300, 8500, and 8800 IP conference devices. HP has fixed the flaw in its Poly Unified Communications Software (UCS) versions 6.4.8 for the VVX devices, 8.1.7 for the Trio 8300, and 7.2.8 for Trio 8500 and 8800.

An exploit module targeting this vulnerability has already been developed and released for the widely used Metasploit penetration testing framework that’s maintained by Rapid7.

The exploit executes code as root on an affected device with ICE enabled by sending a SIP INVITE request with a specially crafted candidate attribute. This attribute normally contains a transport address that can be used for connectivity checks and is part of the ICE RFC8839 standard.

The buffer overflow bug is located in a helper function called ParseICECandidate in the polyapp binary that processes such requests on the device.

“The start of the function contains a call to memcpy , which will copy the incoming string line being processed into a 256 byte stack buffer,” Stephen Fewer, senior principal security researcher at Rapid7, said in a blog post . “No length check is performed to ensure the incoming string length is less than 256 bytes. Therefore by providing a candidate attribute whose length is greater than 256 bytes, a stack-based buffer overflow will occur.”

Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR), a kernel feature that randomizes memory addresses to defeat buffer overflow exploits, is enabled on the device. However, the protection is not operating correctly on the HP Poly devices because it does not randomize the load addresses of .so (Shared Object) libraries.

These libraries, such as libc , are loaded by other processes, including the polyapp process, and because their memory addresses never change, they can be leveraged to bypass ASLR and execute the attacker’s payload.

“We create a ROP chain that will execute an arbitrary OS command via the system standard C library function,” Fewer said. “The accompanying Metasploit exploit modules source code details the entire ROP chain.”

Attackers have increasingly targeted embedded devices inside enterprise networks in recent years because unlike laptops, workstations, and servers, these devices are not monitored by endpoint detection and response (EDR) products. As such, they provide perfect footholds inside corporate environments that allow attackers to remain undetected for long periods of time and attack other systems.

In the age of AI these devices become even more relevant for attackers, going beyond corporate espionage by recording conversations or internal network pivoting.

“Attackers no longer need massive datasets to make use of synthetic speech tooling,” Douglas McKee, Rapid7’s director of vulnerability intelligence, said in a blog post . “In many cases, they just need clean source audio of the right person saying enough words in enough contexts. That has made executive voice data, call recordings, and live conversation capture far more valuable than many organizations seem prepared…

items.title: Leaked EU Draft Would Allow Mass Scanning of Private Messages
items.content:
Leaked EU Draft Would Allow Mass Scanning of Private Messages

A draft proposal puts encrypted chats back under the political microscope.

If you’re tired of censorship and surveillance, subscribe to Reclaim The Net .

Leaked documents have revealed that a secret, unpublished draft deal on the EU’s Child Sexual Abuse Regulation, dubbed Chat Control 2.0 , contains a provision that would allow an “independent administrative authority” (i.e., not a court) to order mass scanning of private messages of all users for up to 24 months at a time, as well as force providers to scan specific parts of their service.

Another revelation is that the Irish Council Presidency, with the Commission’s backing, has been trying to bypass Parliament’s negotiators who have refused to accept this, and instead take the proposal to the group leaders.

This is happening in the context of the trilogue negotiations on Chat Control 2.0, where the seventh, and possibly final, meeting is scheduled for December 8. EU ambassadors (COREPER) are set to meet on December 2.

The document in question is a Council one, numbered WK 16725 2026 INIT, and was drafted by the Parliament’s rapporteur, Javier Zarzalejos (EPP, Spain), and the Irish Presidency. It was made public by Patrick Breyer, a digital rights advocate, who said that the deal breaks both the Council’s and the Parliament’s negotiating mandates by introducing indiscriminate, mandatory mass surveillance of private communications.

According to Breyer, this “independent administrative authority” would be able to issue “detection orders” for the scanning of private messages of all users, with the only limit being that it would have to be for a limited period of 24 months at a time.

This means that European email and chat providers that do not scan today would be forced to do so, while US-based ones would have to use “error-prone AI algorithms to analyze private text chats and ‘unknown’ visuals.”

The “independent administrative authority” would be able to act on its own, without a court order, and issue detection orders whenever a part of the provider’s service has been used for the purpose of child sexual abuse.

The orders could cover “a specific part of the provider’s service, or channel, functionality or other category of communication of that service.” Breyer notes that the scanning of “parts of a service” or “functionalities” is in reality scanning every private message of millions of innocent citizens without individual suspicion, and adds, “In the real world, this would translate to police searching ‘the functionality of envelopes’ to open all letters. It is a semantic trick to rebrand mass surveillance.”

The document’s wording on encryption is such that it excludes “weakening or undermining end-to-end encryption” and “decrypting data” – but it does not rule out client-side scanning, i.e., scanning of messages on the phone before encryption. This means that WhatsApp, which is end-to-end encrypted, could be forced to build this type of scanning into its app.

The Commission’s own impact assessment from 2022 found that detection orders would lead to a 354% increase in reported communications, both true and false. The document also seeks to make “Chat Control 1.0” – voluntary scanning – permanent.

Meanwhile, the Parliament’s position, adopted in November 2023 with a near-unanimous vote, is that scanning should only be allowed of specific suspects and with a judicial warrant, while encryption must be protected and client-side scanning rejected.

All of the Parliament’s negotiators, except for the EPP, refused to sign the text, which prompted the Commission to label them as “extremely intransigent” and call for “unusually robust means and positions” from the Council.

Welcome! This tutorial shows you how to write a small drawing app in Rust, in the spirit of Paint. We open a window, draw rectangles, circles and lines with the mouse, move them around, pick a color, and export the drawing as an image.

We start from an empty cargo new . By the end, you have about 800 lines of Rust spread over fifteen or so files, with a single dependency: minifb , which opens the window and gives us the keyboard and the mouse. Everything else we write ourselves: filling pixels, drawing a line, checking whether the mouse is on a circle, converting an HSV color to RGB.

The tutorial is split into 12 chapters. Each one ends with a program that compiles and does something you can see, even if at first it's just an image file with a red square in it.

I'm a developer and I've been doing data science for several years. But in my free time, I've always been drawn to low-level things: bare metal, and how a computer works at the very bottom of the stack.

I wrote this tutorial with someone in mind who is starting out, or simply curious, and who wonders how a program ends up showing something on the screen. It covers the basics of rasterization, that is, how a rectangle or a circle turns into pixels, starting from nothing and in small pieces you can understand one at a time.

That's mostly what I'd like to show: by moving forward step by step, in a language close to the machine, you end up with something that works and that you wrote entirely yourself. It takes time, but there's nothing magic about it. If this tutorial takes away a bit of that mystery and makes a few beginners want to look further down, it will have done its job.

This tutorial is a way to learn Rust by building something. I assume you've read the first chapters of the Rust Book (variables, functions, if , loops) but haven't written a real program with it yet. The heavier concepts, like enums, traits, borrowing, modules or error handling, come along chapter by chapter, when we need them.

You don't need to know anything about graphics. As for math, you need Pythagoras for circles and a projection to tell whether the mouse is on a line. I explain it when we get there.

Each chapter has boxes that explain why Rust does things the way it does. If you already know, skip them. Same for the exercises at the end of each chapter: they're there if you want practice, but nothing that follows depends on them.

I'd still recommend typing the code rather than copy-pasting it. It's slower, but typing is how you make mistakes, and fixing them is how you end up understanding what the compiler is trying to tell you.

Let's be upfront: at the end, you won't have GIMP. There's no brush, no layers, no undo. And technically, our app isn't even really a Paint. Paint paints pixels that can't be moved once they're down, whereas we keep a list of shapes that can be selected and moved. We come back to this in chapter 11, and the Going further page has ideas for adding a brush, a paint bucket or undo.

01 2D vectors We write a Vec2 type with its operations, and try it out in the terminal. Duration 45 min

02 An image in memory We build an image pixel by pixel and save it in the PPM format. Duration 40 min

03 Drawing shapes We pack each color into a single number, and draw rectangles, circles and lines pixel by pixel. Duration 50 min

04 A window We add our first dependency to open a window and keep showing the canvas in it. Duration 35 min

05 The mouse We draw rectangles by clicking and dragging, with a preview that follows the mouse. Duration 1 h

06 Several shapes We add circles and lines, and choose the tool with the keyboard. Duration 45 min

07 Selecting and moving We click on a shape to select it, drag it to move it, and delete it with the keyboard. Duration 1 h 15

items.title: Against the international oligarchy
items.content:
The explosion of extreme wealth is the major social fact of our time.

Together with more than 100 researchers from around the world (economists, political scientists, legal scholars, sociologists, philosophers, historians and others), we are sounding the alarm: billionaires are a threat to our democracies.

When Forbes magazine began ranking the world’s largest fortunes in 1987, the wealth of the richest 0.0001%, about 1,500 households at the time, amounted to the equivalent of 3% of global gross domestic product.

In 2026, that same tiny fraction of the population, which now comprises nearly 3,000 households as a result of global population growth, holds wealth equal to 17% of global GDP.

This shift has upended the balance of power: the power to steer multinational corporations whose choices, such as the decision to develop artificial intelligence, affect all of humanity; the power to shape the dominant ideology by buying up newspapers, radio stations, television channels and social networks; and the power to sway public policy by funding election campaigns and candidates.

This power is self-reinforcing, in a dynamic that corrupts contemporary democracies. As their economic might has grown, the oligarchs have spent ever more to defend their interests. The economic power of the wealthiest is thus used to strengthen their political power, and vice versa.

Lost from view in the decades after the Second World War, when inequality had fallen to a historic low, the tension between democracy and oligarchy has now fully returned, and is once again asserting itself as the defining issue of our time.

But we cannot understand the terms of this struggle today, nor think through the conditions for a victory of democratic forces, without acknowledging something fundamentally new. For the first time in history, extreme wealth and the power it confers are asserting themselves on a truly planetary scale.

When Elon Musk buys the social network Twitter and puts it at the service of his favored ideological causes, it is not only the American republic that falters; the very terms of public debate, the heart of the democratic life of nations, are transformed in many countries.

When Donald Trump cuts the corporate tax in the United States and dismantles financial transparency rules, it is not only the wealthiest Americans who benefit, but oligarchs the world over, who can make their business in the United States more profitable still.

When a handful of tech barons decide to cover the Earth with data centers that devour energy and water, it is not only the resources of Tennessee or Inner Mongolia that are being seized; it is the planet as a whole that is hurtling toward the abyss.

Extreme wealth always means extreme power, and billionaires are right to point out that their fortunes do not consist mainly of gold bars or cash. They consist of far more than that: above all, control over the course of the world’s major corporations, through the share portfolios they hold, which make up the bulk of their wealth.

Against the international oligarchy, it is a democratic transnational coalition that we must build today.

We propose three complementary pillars to move forward urgently:

1 - Tax justice: a minimum tax on the ultra-rich so that they too contribute their fair share like all of us, combined with the settlement of past unpaid taxes;

2 - Strengthening media independence and the protection of journalists against the risks of interference and censorship in order to consolidate the democratic public sphere;

3 - Democratizing AI governance through a new ownership model—international and de-privatized—for AI companies, along with the democratization of internal corporate governance across the economy.

Through these three pillars, the world’s democratic forces can regain the upper hand. The survival of democracies and the habitability of the planet are at stake. Join us!

items.title: Miasma Worm Targets AI Coding Agents: 73 Microsoft Azure Repos Disabled
items.content:
An unprecedented supply chain attack bypasses registry-level scanners entirely, turning developer tools including Claude Code, Cursor, and Gemini CLI into execution vectors.

The Incident: On June 3, 2026, a highly sophisticated variant of the Miasma worm (also known as Mini Shai-Hulud) launched a coordinated, two-pronged attack targeting both the npm registry and developer source code repositories.

The Escalation: The attack successfully breached multiple high-profile GitHub accounts, including the official Microsoft Azure durabletask repository, using stolen Personal Access Tokens (PATs) and backdated commits to evade traditional audit trails.

The Response: In an ultra-rapid defensive maneuver, GitHub’s automated mitigation systems disabled 73 compromised repositories – including 49 directly associated with Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples within a mere 105-second window .

The Vector: Instead of relying on traditional package installation hooks, Miasma targets the developer’s local environment. It abuses legitimate auto-run, hook, and rule engines within modern IDEs and AI coding assistants ( VS Code, Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI ) to execute a malicious 4.3 MB staged dropper upon folder-open or agent initialization.

The Impact: Once detonated, the Bun-based worm harvests credentials for AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes, npm, and GitHub, and automatically propagates by committing itself back into any repository the victim’s stolen tokens can write to.

At exactly 16:00 UTC on June 3, 2026, a silent, automated purge swept across GitHub. In a high-speed containment action lasting just 105 seconds, 73 active repositories vanished from the platform. Among them were 49 critical repositories belonging to Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples.

This drastic mitigation followed alarming telemetry indicating that threat actors behind the Miasma malware family had regained write access to key cloud repositories. The compromise exploited a stolen Personal Access Token (PAT) belonging to an active Microsoft contributor.

While security firms like StepSecurity and JFrog scrambled to document an concurrent attack vector on the npm registry where 57 malicious packages were published, a second, far more insidious arm of the campaign was already silently spreading directly inside GitHub source repositories.

By bypassing registries and package managers entirely, the Miasma worm targeted the very tools developers use to write code. It didn’t wait for npm install . Instead, it waited for the developer to simply open their code editor or launch an AI coding assistant.

The genius of the Miasma repository-poisoning campaign lies in its exploit surface. When an attacker successfully pushed malicious commits to targeted codebases (such as the popular library icflorescu/mantine-datatable ), the commits added no actual code dependencies.

Instead, the attacker checked in five innocent-looking workspace configuration files and one obfuscated JavaScript file: .github/setup.js .

│ └── settings . json < - - Claude Code SessionStart Hook

│ └── setup . mdc < - - Cursor Agent Prompt Injection

│ └── settings . json < - - Gemini CLI SessionStart Hook

│ └── tasks . json < - - VS Code Automatic Folder - Open Task

├── package . json < -- Hijacked NPM Test Script

└── setup . js < - - The 4.3 MB Staged Dropper

Each of these configuration files is designed to abuse a legitimate, developer-friendly auto-run feature within popular modern tools. Opening the cloned directory in any of these environments instantly triggers execution.

Claude Code & Gemini CLI (SessionStart Hooks)

Both Anthropic’s Claude Code and Google’s Gemini CLI support custom hooks triggered when an AI agent initializes a session in a project workspace. Miasma exploits this by defining a blanket wildcard matcher that forces the agent to execute the dropper via Node.js before any developer prompt is processed.

items.title: usb-rea generates a Linux driver for your Windows-only USB gadget
items.content:
usb-rea is an MIT-licensed tool for people who own a USB gadget that only ships with a Windows program. It captures packets while you use the Windows app and generates a pyusb driver for Linux.

Many years ago, I had to reverse-engineer a USB video capture card, whose vendor didn’t want to work with a company specializing in “small-volume production”. I had to capture the packets with Wireshark and manually implement code to replay URB (USB Request Block) packets using libusb, while paying close attention to timings. A tool like usb-rea would have been useful at the time.

More specifically, usb-rea captures USB traffic with USBPcap or usbmon while the user clicks through the vendor app and labels the actions. The open-source program then infers the command structure (constants, counters, value fields, lookup tables, CRCs) and writes a Markdown protocol report plus a standalone Linux driver.

The developer, Emir Mrkaljevic, already successfully tested it with the NZXT Kraken X AIO liquid cooler and the SteelSeries Rival 100 mouse, both of which are already supported by Linux tools ( liquidctl and rivalcfg ), so verifying the results was easier. usb-rea is notably said to “recover the same fan command liquidctl sends, byte for byte, and the generated driver produces correct packets for values it never saw”. The project can also run as an MCP server, so an AI coding assistant can drive the analysis.

The source code and documentation can be found on GitHub , or you can use pip to install the latest version. It did so on Ubuntu 26.04:

items.title: A Deterministic Subexponential-time Algorithm for the Discrete Logarithm Problem
items.content:
Classical deterministic algorithms for the discrete logarithm problem (DLP) in prime fields $\mathbb{F}_p^*$ and on elliptic curves $E(\mathbb{F}_p)$ require $p^{1/2+o(1)}$ bit operations in the worst case when no unproven number-theoretic hypotheses are assumed. Following the October 2026 refutations of the Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH), Akshima et al. (2026) and Kaarelson (2026) obtained Las Vegas subexponential algorithms for the elliptic-curve discrete logarithm problem over prime fields, while leaving deterministic $p^{o(1)}$ discrete logarithm algorithms open even in $\mathbb{F}_p^*$.

In this paper, we show that assuming the Cauchy--Hermite Boolean tensor contraction construction of OpenAI (October 2026), there is a uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine that solves both the discrete logarithm problem on prime-order elliptic curves over $\mathbb{F}_p$ ($p > 3$) and the discrete logarithm problem in $\mathbb{F}_p^*$ in worst-case time

and space $2^{O(b/(\log b)^{1/4})}$, where $b = \lceil \log_2 p \rceil$. The algorithm uses zero random bits and relies on neither the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis nor smoothness heuristics. Our proof combines two technical ingredients: (i) a deterministic conditional-expectation construction of small affine-interval factor bases whose $2m$-fold sumsets cover the entire group, and (ii) a terminal-preserving partial contraction procedure that bypasses the degree barrier of candidate-label table lookups by compressing the low-degree arithmetic core onto $\Theta(b)$ boundary wires prior to exact digitwise contraction.

All the theorems/lemmas have passed the Lean verification on https://prove2.me/missions/A_Deterministic_Subexponential-time_Algorithm_for_the_Discrete_Logarithm_Problem .

Three skills in this plugin (listed in Anthropic's claude-plugins-official marketplace) raised the same concern for me:

Together with an unpinned script from a generated-name host, a user has no way to review what runs.

convex-backend-skill/skills/quickstart/SKILL.md

convex-backend-skill/skills/add/SKILL.md

convex-backend-skill/skills/labs-quickstart/SKILL.md

items.title: Meta’s Content Moderation Said to Be Severely Broken After Moving to Human Reviewers to AI: "It's been really a mess."
items.content:
Content moderation at Meta, the world’s biggest social media company, is extremely broken amid a push to cut human staff in favor of AI systems.

Meta employees told The Guardian that the social media giant’s push to use AI to automate content moderation systems while slashing human moderation jobs has been a “mess,” as the AI systems frequently fail to understand nuance and remove content they shouldn’t. Remaining employees are left trying to moderate Meta’s massive platforms with “skeleton teams,” some of which have just two-thirds or even half the staff they used to, employees said.

“It’s been really a mess,” one Meta insider told the Guardian , who also said that they’ve repeatedly tried to get in touch with certain teams to discuss an issue, but discovered in the process that those teams were completely disbanded.

To offset the lack of humans, Meta has turned to AI systems to help moderate its platforms. But Meta staff told the Guardian that these systems have a hard time understanding nuance, particularly in non-English languages. Posts are often taken down that shouldn’t be, and users impacted by bad moderation have a more difficult time fixing the issue than before.

“You are trying to gut all human reviewers, which are kind of essential for making these nuanced decisions and policy decisions,” one Meta employee told the Guardian. “Of course there are going to be mistakes that are going to happen.”

“Even if you know someone at Meta, it’s still very difficult to get through to someone who’s actually going to be able to help you, especially if it’s a highly nuanced case,” the employee added. “It’s so much more difficult now.”

In a statement, Meta refuted the claim that its content moderation system is dysfunctional, telling the Guardian that “everyone on our platforms is subject to the same set of rules, and any claims of enforcement based on political affiliation or advocacy are baseless.”

“While we have long used AI to help enforce our community standards, earlier this year we began experimenting with more advanced AI systems that can more quickly and accurately catch violations with fewer mistakes,” the statement continued. “The latest tests show that on average these systems make 13 percent fewer mistakes than humans when enforcing against violating content, while finding 10 percent more actual violations — and we give people opportunity to appeal decisions if they think we’ve got it wrong.”

As the Guardian notes, Meta has historically tried to cut costs by outsourcing content moderation work to human teams in Kenya. Meta’s longtime moderation partner in Africa, SAMA, has been referred to as a “ sweatshop ” due to mistreatment of its minimally-paid staffers, who are tasked with keeping social media sites clear of some of the most disturbing content imaginable.

Recent Futurism reporting has found that Meta is failing to remove abusive content such as AI-generated videos of physical child abuse and sexual abuse of girls and young women from its platforms, even when users directly report them.

More on Meta’s content moderation: Meta Is Refusing to Remove AI-Generated Videos of Coaches Inappropriately Touching Young Athletes When Users Report Them

items.title: False computer-checked proofs
items.content:
There are some computer programs that claim to check every step in a proof.

various "soundness bugs" have been reported that at least potentially allowed false statements to slip past these programs.

these bugs have been demonstrated to be exploitable.

The list at the bottom of this page links to what appear to be reports of soundness bugs

for various important proof-checking programs,

sorted in increasing order of the number of reports.

This list includes many more soundness bugs for these programs than the bugs mentioned in

and I don't think the list is missing any of the bugs mentioned there,

Please let me know about any corrections or additions.

Beware that this list doesn't include user-interface vulnerabilities.

Those can have the same important effect of misleading a user as to what has been proven.

One standard path towards security is to minimize the complexity of the trusted computing base,

which by definition is the part of the system that security reviewers need to check.

HOL Light's proof-checking kernel is attractive because of its stability and simplicity, only 400 lines of code.

But this size measurement doesn't say how carefully the HOL Light code has been reviewed,

and doesn't say anything about the possibility of bugs in the underlying programming language.

Extra code can be good when it's test code.

A battery of tests tends to catch more bugs than a single test.

Running a proof through multiple proof-checking programs

(preferably each in its own isolated environment)

can save the day when there's a bug in one program,

and is particularly easy if the checkers take the same input language for writing proofs.

But it's not clear how effective this is at stopping attacks:

is better answered by a proof saying that a checker works correctly.

A close translation of the inference rules in the HOL Light kernel,

except for the rules to introduce new definitions,

We're working with the Garage Door Up as much as we can here, and I felt like this is an angle/experience that a) is real, it happens b) isn't mentioned that often.

(if you know/are a designer/developer/tinkerer who prototypes their work with poems -- let me know about them or Say Hi !)

To which he said stroking his yellow beard:

This something else was Gentle Worms ( Getting / Racing Worms? working title!). The idea is simple: instead of using alarms to track time, we fire gentle visual notifications that appear gradually on the screen. Superficially it's similar to Pickle (a metronome for attention).
